summary: A quarter is one of FOUR EQUAL parts of a whole. Reach quarters by repeated halving (fold in half, then halve each half, giving four matching parts in total), work them on single objects, lengths, and sets (a quarter of 12 = share into four equal groups and take one), and show that four quarters recompose the whole while two quarters make a half — seeding equivalence. The core learner actions are partitioning/folding to make equal parts and sharing a set into four equal groups, with naming and counting attached to the number of equal parts.
misconceptions: Any four pieces count as quarters regardless of size (equal-parts missing)
Muddling the names — calling a quarter 'a half', or vice versa
A quarter of a set found by making groups OF four rather than four equal groups
Thinking a quarter is bigger than a half because 'four is more than two' (whole-number bias, developing here)

activities.title: Halve, then halve again: making four equal quarters
steps: Fold (or partition) a symmetrical shape such as a square, rectangle or circle in half, then fold each half in half again so the shape opens into four matching parts.
Check the four parts are equal by matching or overlaying them; only equal parts count as quarters.
Count aloud: 'four quarters make one whole'.
Join two of the quarters to make a half, then place that pair over the other two quarters (or over an identical shape folded once into halves) to see that 'two quarters make a half'.
Compare with a shape cut into four UNEQUAL pieces and explain why those are not quarters.
activities.insight: A quarter is one of four EQUAL parts; repeated halving is a reliable way to produce them, four quarters rebuild the whole, and two quarters together make a half.

activities.title: A quarter of a set: sharing 12 into four equal groups
steps: Take 12 counters and share them, one at a time, into four equal groups (four hoops or circles).
Keep going until all 12 are placed and every group has the same number.
Report how many are in one group — 'a quarter of 12 is 3'.
Contrast with making groups OF four and notice that gives three groups, which is a different question.
activities.insight: A quarter of a set is found by sharing the whole set into four equal groups and taking one group — not by making groups of four.

activities.title: Naming by counting equal parts: halves vs quarters
steps: Partition one shape into two equal parts and name each a 'half'; partition another into four equal parts and name each a 'quarter'.
Count the equal parts aloud and attach the name to the count: two equal parts = halves, four equal parts = quarters.
Use halve-then-halve-again on the same shape to see how a half becomes two quarters.
Decide, for a correctly-made part, whether it is a half or a quarter and justify by counting the equal parts.
activities.insight: The fraction name follows the number of equal parts: two equal parts are halves, four equal parts are quarters; of the SAME whole, a quarter is smaller than a half.

activities.title: Sorting quarters from not-quarters
steps: Look at several shapes and sets, some divided into four EQUAL parts and some into four UNEQUAL parts.
Sort each into 'quarters' or 'not quarters', including a tricky case cut into four clearly unequal pieces.
For each 'not quarters' case, say what is wrong (the parts are not equal) and how to fix it (fold in half then half again, or divide into four equal parts).
Answer: 'A quarter of 12 is ___' and explain how you know.
activities.insight: Having four pieces is not enough — the four parts must be equal to be quarters.

checkQuestion: Show a square divided into four pieces that are clearly different sizes. Ask: 'Is each of these pieces a quarter of the square? How do you know?' Then ask: 'How could you fold a square to be sure of making four quarters, and how many quarters make the whole square?'
checkAnswer: No - the pieces are not equal, so they are not quarters. Quarters are four EQUAL parts; fold in half and then in half again (or divide into four equal parts) so all four match. Four equal quarters make the whole square.
